blocks.text: Every time you train a model, randomness is quietly doing a lot of the work. The starting weights of your network, the order your training examples get shuffled in, which rows end up in your test set, which neurons get dropped during training, all of it comes from calls into NumPy's random number generation tools. If you don't control that randomness on purpose, your experiments become impossible to repeat, and debugging turns into chasing a ghost. This lesson walks through numpy.random end to end: the modern recommended way to generate random numbers, why it replaced the old approach, how seeding gives you full reproducibility, and the handful of generator methods you will reach for constantly as an ML engineer.

blocks.caption: Randomness shows up at almost every stage of a typical ML pipeline.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973285-516479885.png
1. Introduction

It helps to name the exact places randomness shows up before diving into the API itself. Once you see the list, you'll notice that "random" in ML almost never means "arbitrary." It means "drawn from a controlled process so the model doesn't learn some accidental pattern in how the data happened to be ordered or initialized."

items: Weight initialization: a network's weights start as small random numbers, usually drawn from a normal or uniform distribution, so different neurons don't all learn the exact same thing.
Shuffling datasets: rows get reshuffled before each training epoch so the model doesn't memorize the order examples happen to appear in.
Train and test splits: which rows land in training versus testing is a random decision, and it needs to be a decision you can repeat.
Dropout: during training, a random subset of neurons gets temporarily switched off on each pass, which helps prevent overfitting.
Data augmentation: random crops, rotations, and flips applied to images, or random word swaps in text, all rely on the same random number tools.
Sampling: picking a random batch from a large dataset, or sampling a subset of rows for a quick experiment, both come down to random selection.

blocks.text: All of these rely on the same underlying toolkit: numpy.random. NumPy actually ships two different ways to reach for randomness, an older one built around global shared state, and a newer one built around an explicit generator object. Understanding the difference between them is not just trivia, it directly affects whether your experiments are reproducible.

blocks.title: What this lesson covers
blocks.content: You will see both the legacy global state API and the modern Generator API, understand exactly why the modern one is preferred, learn how seeding gives you reproducibility, and walk through the core generator methods you'll use constantly: random, integers, normal, choice, shuffle, and permutation.

blocks.text: 2. Modern vs Legacy Random APIs

NumPy has carried two parallel ways of generating random numbers for years. New code should almost always reach for the modern one, but you will still run into the legacy one constantly in older codebases, tutorials, and papers' reference implementations, so it's worth understanding both.
2.1 The Legacy Global State API

The original NumPy random API works by calling functions directly on the numpy.random module, like np.random.rand() or np.random.randint(). Underneath, these functions all read from and write to one single, shared, global random state that lives inside the module itself. You seed that global state with np.random.seed(42), and from that point on, every call anywhere in your program pulls the next number out of that same shared stream.

code.content:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)
print(np.random.rand())      # 0.3745401188473625
print(np.random.randint(10)) # 9

# both calls above advanced the SAME global stream
print(np.random.rand())      # a different number again, drawn from that shared state

blocks.caption: The legacy API funnels every call, from every part of your program, through one shared mutable object.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973285-8714973.png

The trouble is that this global state is shared by literally everything: your own code, any library you import that also happens to call NumPy's legacy random functions, even a testing framework running in the background. If two unrelated pieces of code both draw from that same global stream, the order in which they happen to run changes what numbers each one gets. Reorder an import, add an extra print statement that triggers a random call somewhere, or upgrade a dependency that now calls np.random once more than it used to, and your "reproducible" seeded run quietly stops being reproducible.

blocks.title: Gotcha: the legacy API is a shared mutable singleton
blocks.content: Calling np.random.seed() resets state that every other consumer of numpy.random also reads from. Two libraries, or even two unrelated modules in your own project, drawing from that same stream can silently interfere with each other. This is exactly the class of bug that the modern Generator API was built to eliminate.

blocks.text: 2.2 The Modern Generator API

The modern approach starts with np.random.default_rng(), which returns a Generator object. That object holds its own private random state, separate from the legacy global module state and separate from every other Generator you create. You call methods directly on that object, like rng.random() or rng.integers(), instead of calling functions on the module.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
print(rng.random())      # 0.7739560485559633
print(rng.integers(10))  # 7

# a second, independent generator, completely unaffected by the one above
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
print(rng2.random())     # its own separate sequence

blocks.caption: Each Generator instance owns its own state. Nothing outside it can disturb its sequence of draws.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973286-744037654.png

Notice that rng and rng2 above never touch each other. You can pass rng around your codebase, into a data loader, a model initializer, a shuffling function, and every one of those pieces of code shares that exact same, deliberately shared, generator instance if you want them to, or gets its own fresh one if you don't. Either way, it's an explicit choice you make, not an accident of import order.
2.3 Why the Modern Generator Is Preferred

The core difference comes down to state ownership. The legacy API forces every consumer of randomness in your program to share one object whether they want to or not. The modern API lets each part of your code hold its own isolated, independently seeded generator, so behavior in one place can never leak into another place by accident.

blocks.text: In practice this means new NumPy code, and any ML code you write today, should create a Generator with default_rng() right at the start and pass that single object wherever randomness is needed, rather than calling np.random.seed() once and hoping every downstream function behaves.
3. Reproducibility via Seeding

Reproducibility is the entire point of seeding. A seed is just a starting number you hand to default_rng(). Every "random" number that generator produces afterward is actually the output of a deterministic algorithm running on that starting number, so the exact same seed always produces the exact same sequence of draws, every single time, on every machine.

blocks.caption: The same seed, used the same way, always produces the same sequence, no matter how many times you run it.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973286-84018548.png

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=7)
print([rng.integers(100) for _ in range(5)])   # [26, 39, 78, 8, 30]

rng_again = np.random.default_rng(seed=7)
print([rng_again.integers(100) for _ in range(5)])   # [26, 39, 78, 8, 30]  identical

blocks.text: This matters enormously in ML work. When a model behaves oddly, being able to rerun the exact same training loop and get the exact same weight initialization, the exact same shuffle order, and the exact same dropout mask lets you actually isolate what changed. Without a fixed seed, every rerun is a different experiment, and you can never be fully sure whether a fix actually fixed anything or the result just got lucky this time. Seeding is also what lets a teammate, or a reviewer, or your future self six months from now, rerun your experiment and land on the same numbers you reported.
3.1 What a Seed Actually Does

A seed initializes the internal state of the generator's underlying algorithm. Nothing NumPy produces is truly random in the physical sense, it is pseudorandom: a long, well distributed sequence of numbers that looks random to any statistical test, but is fully determined by that one starting seed. Give the same seed to the same version of NumPy, and you get the same sequence back, guaranteed.

blocks.title: Pseudorandom, not truly random
blocks.content: This determinism is a feature, not a limitation. It is exactly what makes seeded random number generation useful for science and engineering: you get numbers that behave statistically like randomness, while still being fully reproducible whenever you need them to be.

blocks.text: 3.2 When to Avoid True Randomness

If you call np.random.default_rng() with no seed at all, NumPy pulls entropy from the operating system to seed itself, and you get a genuinely different sequence on every run. During active model development, that is almost always the wrong choice.

blocks.caption: Skipping the seed during development turns every bug into a moving target.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973286-26950798.png

Picture debugging a training run that occasionally produces exploding gradients. Without a fixed seed, every attempt to reproduce the failure uses a completely different weight initialization and a completely different shuffle order, so the bug shows up on some runs and vanishes on others for no reason you can pin down. With a fixed seed, you can rerun the exact same conditions as many times as you need, add print statements, step through with a debugger, and trust that any change in behavior came from your code change, not from a new roll of the dice.

blocks.title: A practical rule of thumb
blocks.content: Fix a seed for every experiment while you are developing and debugging. Once a model is fully validated and you are running final production training, it is reasonable to use a fresh, unseeded run, or a randomly chosen seed that you log and report alongside your results, so the final numbers reflect genuine variation rather than one lucky roll.

blocks.text: 4. Core Distributions and Generator Methods

With a Generator object in hand, a handful of methods cover almost everything you'll need day to day as an ML engineer: drawing uniform floats, drawing random integers, drawing from a normal distribution, sampling from an existing array, and shuffling data. Each one is covered below with a small, focused example.
4.1 Uniform Floats with rng.random
rng.random() returns a float sampled uniformly from the half open interval zero to one, meaning zero is a possible result but one is not. Pass a shape to get back an entire array of them at once.

code.content:
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

single = rng.random()          # 0.5118216247145734
batch = rng.random(size=5)     # array of 5 floats, each in [0.0, 1.0)

blocks.caption: rng.random gives you plain uniform floats, the building block behind most other distributions.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973287-324977070.png
4.2 Random Integers with rng.integers

rng.integers(low, high) returns a random integer from low up to but not including high. This is what you reach for whenever you need a random index, a random batch size, or a random count of anything.

code.content:
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

one_die_roll = rng.integers(1, 7)          # an integer from 1 through 6
random_indices = rng.integers(0, 1000, size=8)   # 8 random integers, each from 0 up to 999

blocks.caption: rng.integers is the go to method whenever you need a random index or count.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973619-12786310.png
4.3 Normal Draws with rng.normal

rng.normal(loc, scale) draws from a normal, or Gaussian, distribution, where loc is the mean and scale is the standard deviation. This is the distribution behind most weight initialization schemes: you want a network's starting weights to be small random numbers clustered around zero, not wildly spread out, so training starts from a stable place.

code.content:
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

weights = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.05, size=(4, 3))
# a 4 by 3 matrix of weights, centered around 0.0, mostly within about 0.15 of it

blocks.caption: rng.normal is the distribution behind almost every weight initialization scheme in deep learning.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973620-519611339.png

blocks.title: Why normal, and why small
blocks.content: Real initialization schemes like Xavier or He initialization are really just rng.normal with a carefully chosen scale that depends on the layer's size. The math behind choosing that scale is a topic of its own, but the underlying draw is exactly this method.

blocks.text: 4.4 Sampling with rng.choice

rng.choice(array, size, replace) picks random elements out of an existing array. With replace=True, the same element can be picked more than once. With replace=False, every picked element is unique, which is what you want for sampling a subset of rows without duplicating any of them.

code.content:
data = np.array(['cat', 'dog', 'fish', 'bird', 'lion'])
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

with_dupes = rng.choice(data, size=8, replace=True)     # may repeat entries
no_dupes = rng.choice(data, size=3, replace=False)      # 3 distinct entries, never repeated

blocks.caption: Whether replace is true or false decides if the same item can be picked twice.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973621-739603905.png
4.5 Shuffling In Place vs Permutation

rng.shuffle(array) reorders an array's elements randomly, but it does so in place: the original array itself gets modified, and the method returns nothing. rng.permutation(array) does the same kind of reordering, but instead returns a brand new shuffled array and leaves the original untouched.

code.content:
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)

original = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
rng.shuffle(original)
print(original)          # the original array, now reordered

rng2 = np.random.default_rng(seed=1)
source = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
shuffled_copy = rng2.permutation(source)
print(source)            # unchanged: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
print(shuffled_copy)     # a new, separately reordered array

blocks.caption: Same idea, different contracts: shuffle mutates, permutation returns something new.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973621-621469099.png

blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: Reproducible Train Test Split

Here is all of this put together in the exact shape you'll use it in practice: splitting a dataset into training and testing sets, in a way that is fully reproducible because it is driven by one seeded generator.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# pretend we have 1000 rows of training data
num_rows = 1000
X = np.arange(num_rows)   # stand in for your actual feature rows

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)

# shuffle a plain index array instead of shuffling X directly,
# so we can apply the exact same order to labels later too
indices = np.arange(num_rows)
rng.shuffle(indices)

split_point = int(num_rows * 0.8)
train_indices = indices[:split_point]
test_indices = indices[split_point:]

X_train = X[train_indices]
X_test = X[test_indices]

print(len(X_train), len(X_test))   # 800 200
print(X_train[:5])                 # first 5 rows of the shuffled training set

# rerun with the same seed, and you get the exact same split every time
rng_repeat = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
indices_repeat = np.arange(num_rows)
rng_repeat.shuffle(indices_repeat)
print(np.array_equal(indices, indices_repeat))   # True

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Reproducible Train Test Split
blocks.caption: Shuffle the index array with a seeded generator, then slice it. Anyone with the same seed gets the same split.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441973622-833637949.png

Shuffling the index array, rather than shuffling the feature array directly, is a small habit worth adopting. It means you can apply that exact same shuffled order to labels, to a second array of extra features, or to anything else tied row for row to your dataset, and everything stays perfectly aligned.

blocks.title: Keep one generator, or one seed, per experiment
blocks.content: Create a single rng at the top of your training script and pass it into every function that needs randomness: initialization, shuffling, splitting, augmentation. Log the seed value alongside your results. That combination is what makes an experiment fully reproducible from a bare script.

blocks.text: 6. Wrap Up

Randomness in NumPy is not a side detail, it is load bearing infrastructure for almost everything you do in ML engineering. The modern default_rng() approach gives you an isolated, independently seeded Generator instance instead of a shared global state that anything in your process can quietly disturb. Seeding that generator is what turns "random" into "reproducible," which is exactly what you need while developing, debugging, and sharing results with other people.

items: Prefer default_rng over the legacy np.random.seed plus module level functions for all new code.
A Generator instance owns its own state, so it cannot be disturbed by other libraries or other parts of your codebase.
The same seed always produces the same sequence of draws, which is essential for debugging and for others reproducing your results.
rng.random gives uniform floats, rng.integers gives random integers, rng.normal gives Gaussian draws used constantly for weight init.
rng.choice samples from an existing array, with or without replacement, depending on whether duplicates are acceptable.
rng.shuffle reorders in place and returns nothing, rng.permutation returns a new shuffled copy and leaves the original untouched.
Fix a seed during development. Consider an unseeded or logged random seed only for a final production run.

blocks.text: Once this becomes second nature, reproducibility stops being something you have to think hard about. It just falls out of always creating one seeded generator per experiment and threading it through every place your code needs a random number.
